To immigrate means to move into a foreign country with the intention of living there permanently (or for a long time).

The action has two key parts baked into it:

  • You are leaving your home country behind.
  • You are entering and settling in a new country.

Think of it this way: the word carries the idea of crossing into a new land to make it your new home — not just to visit, but to stay.

"Thousands of people immigrate to Canada every year."

This means thousands of people are arriving in Canada and making it their new permanent home.
The Direction of Movement

This is the most important thing to lock into your memory:

"Immigrate" is always told from the perspective of the destination country — the country you are moving INTO.

So when you say someone immigrated, you are focusing on their arrival and settlement in the new place.

"She immigrated to Australia in 2005." → She came to Australia and settled there.
What Makes It Different from Just "Moving"

Not every move counts as immigration. Three conditions are usually true when this word is used:

  1. A national border is crossed. You move from one country to a different country. Moving from one city to another within the same country is not immigration.
  2. The purpose is to live there. A tourist visiting for two weeks is not immigrating. A student on a short course is generally not immigrating. The intent to reside — to build a life there — is what matters.
  3. It is (mostly) a human action. We use this word for people, not for animals. (Animals that move between regions are said to migrate, a different word.)
Immigrate vs. Emigrate — The Twin That Confuses Everyone

These two words describe the exact same physical journey, but from opposite viewpoints.

  • Emigrate = to leave your home country. (Focus: the country you are departing from.)
  • Immigrate = to arrive and settle in a new country. (Focus: the country you are going to.)

Imagine a person named Ali who is born in Egypt and moves to Germany to live:

  • From Egypt's point of view → Ali emigrated from Egypt.
  • From Germany's point of view → Ali immigrated to Germany.
  • Ali himself could say either, depending on which part of the journey he's describing.

A simple memory trick: Immigrate = move in. Emigrate = exit.
How the Verb Changes Form

SituationFormExample
  • Base form: immigrate → "Many people want to immigrate."
  • Present (he/she/it): immigrates → "She immigrates next month."
  • Past: immigrated → "His grandparents immigrated in the 1950s."
  • Ongoing action: immigrating → "They are currently immigrating."
What Comes After "Immigrate" in a Sentence

The verb immigrate is almost always followed by the word "to" and then the name of the destination country or place:

  • immigrate to the United States
  • immigrate to a new country
  • immigrate to Europe

Occasionally, you will see "from" added as well to show where the person came from:

  • "He immigrated to Brazil from Portugal."

You will almost never see "immigrate" used without a destination. The destination is the heart of the word.
Common Collocations (Words That Naturally Pair With It)

These are real phrases you will frequently encounter:

  • legally immigrate → to move to a country through the official, government-approved process.
  • immigrate for work / for a better life / for safety → shows the reason for immigrating.
  • plan/hope/decide to immigrate → used when talking about future intentions.
  • immigrate with one's family → moving together as a unit.
The Word Family (Related Words)

Knowing these will help you recognize the word in all its forms:

  • Immigrant (noun) → the person who immigrates. "She is an immigrant."
  • Immigration (noun) → the process or phenomenon of people immigrating. "Immigration has shaped this country's culture."
  • Immigrate (verb) → the action itself. "They immigrated ten years ago."
A Few Sentences to See It in Action

1. "After years of planning, my uncle finally immigrated to the Netherlands."
  2. "It is not easy to immigrate to a country whose language you don't speak."
  3. "Her family immigrated from Vietnam to the United States when she was just three years old."
  4. "The government made it harder to immigrate legally."
  5. "He always dreamed of immigrating somewhere with a warmer climate."
The One-Sentence Summary

To immigrate = to move from your home country into a new country, with the intention of living there.

Everything else in this explanation is just detail layered on top of that single truth. If you remember nothing else, remember this: immigrate is about coming in to stay.
